title: Energy and productive capacity

blocks.heading: Energy and productive capacity
blocks.text: Energy supports productive activities such as transport, heating, pumping and operating machinery. Sources differ in availability, reliability, costs and environmental effects. Choosing energy for development requires matching the source and supply arrangement to the productive need rather than treating any one source as universally best. A daylight water-pumping task and continuous overnight refrigeration need different supply arrangements. A source that works well for the first may need storage or backup for the second. Compare the actual service delivered, maintenance capacity and effects over time. The following sources explain options without predicting current prices or future national supply.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Oil
blocks.text: Oil is a non-renewable fossil resource used to produce fuels for transport, machinery and other activities. Liquid fuels can be transported and stored, but continued use depends on supply and creates combustion emissions. A diesel-powered delivery vehicle can carry produce where fuel is available. Imports or interrupted deliveries may create a supply constraint. Oil is a finite stock on human timescales; refining or storing it does not make it renewable. Avoid equating the convenience of a fuel with an absence of environmental costs.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Coal
blocks.text: Coal is a non-renewable fossil fuel used to provide heat and generate electricity. Coal-based energy requires fuel supply and creates pollution and greenhouse-gas emissions when burned. A production activity may use electricity generated from coal without burning coal at the workshop itself. Distinguish the energy service from the upstream source. Reliable electricity can support output, while fuel extraction, transport and emissions remain relevant to a development judgement.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Nuclear energy
blocks.text: Nuclear energy uses energy released from nuclear fuel to generate electricity; the fuel is treated as non-renewable in this syllabus grouping. Nuclear generation can provide sustained electricity, but requires specialist capacity, high initial investment and careful safety and radioactive-waste management. It does not burn fossil fuel during electricity generation, which distinguishes it from coal and gas combustion. That does not mean it has no environmental or safety issues. Understand its productive role and trade-offs here; reactor engineering and nuclear physics are outside this topic.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Natural gas
blocks.text: Natural gas is a non-renewable fossil fuel used for heating and electricity generation. Combustion produces emissions, and leaks and supply infrastructure matter to its environmental and practical effects. Gas is not renewable merely because it is called natural. A gas-fired supply can support production where fuel and infrastructure are available, but users depend on that supply. Classify a source by how it is replenished, not by whether its name sounds environmentally friendly.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Solar energy
blocks.text: Solar energy uses incoming sunlight, for example through photovoltaic panels that generate electricity. Output depends on available sunlight; a task needing power outside those conditions requires a suitable storage or complementary supply arrangement. A daylight pump may use solar electricity directly, whereas night-time refrigeration needs an arrangement that bridges the hours without sunlight. Initial equipment, maintenance and local repair capacity also matter. A renewable source is not a claim that energy is available at every moment or at no cost.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Biogas
blocks.text: Biogas is a combustible gas produced when suitable organic matter decomposes without oxygen in a controlled system. It can use organic wastes as an energy feedstock, but needs a dependable feedstock, water and suitable operation and maintenance. An invented livestock group may use collected manure in a managed digester. Naming biogas is insufficient if the group lacks enough feedstock or cannot maintain the system. Its biological source differs from natural gas, which is a finite fossil resource in this classification.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Wood fuel
blocks.text: Wood can provide heat and is renewable where regrowth replaces harvesting under suitable conditions. Extraction faster than regeneration can reduce the stock, while inefficient burning can waste fuel and contribute to smoke pollution. The development issue includes access to useful heat, woodland condition and the efficiency of the stove or process. Planting seedlings without protecting them or controlling excessive harvesting may not maintain supply. Carry the regeneration condition with any claim that wood use is sustainable.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Hydroelectric power
blocks.text: Hydroelectric power uses moving or falling water to drive turbines that generate electricity. Its output depends on suitable water flow and infrastructure; water variability and impacts on ecosystems and communities affect its development role. The water cycle renews the source, but available flow can vary by season or drought. A dam or generating station also requires investment and maintenance. Do not assume that a renewable classification makes all locations suitable or removes social and environmental trade-offs.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Match the supply to the task
blocks.text: A fictional garden pumps water during daylight and has space to store the water. Its fuel deliveries are unreliable, but suitable sunlight, equipment finance and repair support are available. A solar pump could reduce exposure to the fuel-delivery interruption while storing water bridges the watering schedule. This does not prove solar alone would suit a workshop requiring continuous power overnight. That task would need a reliable arrangement for hours without sunlight. Compare total service, supply conditions, maintenance and environmental effects rather than merely attaching renewable or non-renewable labels.
